During radio's infancy, AM broadcast stations reigned; not just in the United States, but in Europe and elsewhere in the world.
INTRODUCTIONM

The developers of the emerging radio technology were well aware that AM lacked any innate immunity to noise. Further, all efforts to alter the operating characteristics of AM as a way of providing it with resistance to noise was, at best, unfruitful.

Noise reduction was extemely important, especially for communications. In 1936, the first practical FM system was tested. Since then, FM has provided a realistic solution to broadcast and communications radio technology..of FM was initiated.

LESSON MENU
FREQUENCY MODULATION
Unlike Amplitude Modulation, where amplitude is the modulating component in the signal and frequency remains constant; in Frequency Modulation, amplitude is constant while frequency is modulated.
DISCUSSION
This means the "intelligence" is carried in minute, instantaneous variations in the frequency.
While this is the obvious difference between AM and FM, there are many other benefits and deficits between the two forms of modulation. Some are more apparent than others.
AM transmissions actually produce 3 frequencies: the carrier (or center frequency) and 2 sidebands, an upper and a lower.
Frequency modulation presents an entirely different picture mathematically because it has the carrier as well as an infinite number of sidebands.
For example, when a frequency modulated signal is derived from a 5 kHz modulating frequency, the resultant frequency will have sidebands at 5 kHz intervals to infinity.
The sidebands, as they progress outward in either direction from the carrier, will continually become weaker and weaker; but, none-the-less, are still present.
Those sidebands that contain the majority of the power are considered significant sidebands.
This, of course, makes FM a far more complex form of modulation than AM. It also is the factor that indicates the need for some sort of limiting device.
FM sidebands have equal amplitudes and are always an equal distance from the carrier frequency. This keeps FM sideband distribution in a symmetrical format around the carrier frequency.

Here are some additional observations pertinent to frequency modulated signals: 1. When a carrier frequency is modulated, its power is reduced. 2. Any energy removed from the carrier is added to the sidebands. 3. The greater the amplitude of the modulating signal, the more power produced in the sidebands. 4. Most people are aware that their home receiver is far quieter when switched to FM as opposed to AM. Static noise is not commonly heard in the FM band, whereas, with AM it can be quite noisy.

Noise is seen in the form of amplitude variations. We know from previous lessons that the intelligence in an AM signal is located in the USB and LSB which is the same as saying that the intelligence is stored in the amplitude variations of the carrier frequency. Obviously, then, any introduction of noise will have a dramatic affect on the detected sign.
The removal of noise spikes in an FM signal is accomplished by the limiter circuitry. Outwardly, this may appear to be without cost. However, there is a trade-off.

While the limiter is capable of clipping off a noise spike, the spike still generates a phase shift. This phase shift causes a shift in the frequency which cannot be compensated for. Fortunately, this deviation in frequency caused by the noise is rarely an audible problem.
Because of the selective characteristics of the tuning circuitry in an FM receiver, the frequency range of the noise will be very close to the desired tuned FM signal.

That is, if the receiver is tuned to 89.9 MHz, the gain provided by the receiver's amplifiers for the tuned frequency will also provide amplification to any noise at or near 89.9 MHz. The noise (although clipped) has sufficient energy to cause phase shift and thus, frequency deviation.
The advantage of reduced noise in FM transmissions is actually a trade-off. AM signals occupy a 10 kHz bandwidth within their assigned frequency range. FM signals have bandwidths of
200 kHz for broadcast transmissions and about 30 kHz for narrow-band FM used for voice communications.

Simple math tells you that twenty AM stations take up the same space in the frequency spectrum as just one FM station. This is necessary because the power in FM signals is located in its multiple sidebands.

Remember that the power in an AM signal is located in its upper and lower sideband which is only 5 kHz above and below the 455 kHz IFsignal. The sidebands in FM are directly proportional to the modulating frequency and are spaced apart at the same frequency.

Aside from relatively noiseless reception, the greatest benefit of FM broadcasts for most people is stereophonic sound.
It was the appearance of stereo records and tapes in the late 1950's that was the driving force for the development of stereo FM broadcasts.

Stereo transmission and reception is far more complex because two separate audio signals must be used to modulate the same carrier while, at the same time, occupy different frequency ranges. This is accomplished through the use of a sub-carrier and frequency-division multiplexing.
In order to transmit in stereo, both a left channel (L) and a right channel (R) must be created in the recording studio or concert hall. Simplified FM Stereo Generator
The left and right channels are fed into a Summing/Difference amplifier (commonly referred to as a matrix) to produce a left minus right channel (L - R) and a left plus right channel (L + R).

Since the (L + R) sideband is a frequency that can easily be filtered at the receiver; no further processing is required. The signal is directly transmitted through the summing network. The (L - R) signal requires additional modification.

A 19 kHz pilot sub-carrier is sent simultaneously to the summing network (used as a reference signal) and to the frequency doubler. From the doubler, the now 38 kHz signal and the (L - R) signal are modulated and also sent to the summing network. The (L + R), modified (L - R) and pilot signal constitute the composite stereo signal that is ultimately transmitted and received.

On the receiving end, the composite FM stereo signal (having been conditioned by filters and amplifiers) has its three components separated by filters and then processed. Simplified FM Stereo Decoding Circuitry
Because the (L + R) signal was not modified, all that is needed to extract it from the composite signal is a low pass filter. A band-pass filter extracts the 19 kHz pilot frequency.
A high frequency band-pass filter is used to extract the

23 - 53 kHz carrier signal which contains the intelligence from the (L - R) signal. The pilot frequency is then doubled again and modulated with the carrier signal. In the process, the (L - R) signal is extracted.
The two signals are then fed into the summing/difference (matrix) amplifier where the (L - R) is added to the (L + R) signal to produce a 2L signal. The (L + R) signal is subtracted from the

These two signals are then sent to their appropriate audio amplifiers. This process also allows normal reception for non-stereophonic FM receivers. An FM stereophonic system requires stringent technological management. This is particularly true with the generation and transmission aspects.
It should be mentioned that some AM radio stations are also broadcasting in stereo. Several methods of stereophonic amplitude modulation were devised in the late 1970's.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC), however, elected to defer to the marketplace the choice of which system is best. Subsequently, as of 1987, there were only 400 AM stations broadcasting in stereo in the United States, using four different systems. This has resulted in FM radio taking a firm lead as the mode of choice in broadcast radio.

One of the problems overcome by FM broadcasts is interference between stations operating at or near the same frequency. In order for radio coverage to be as complete as possible, station broadcast areas sometimes overlap.

Nighttime AM broadcasts are particularly subject to this problem because of variations in the depth of the ionosphere, for example, the disappearance of the E layer, which allows skywaves to be reflected great distances. When listening to an AM radio, it is not uncommon to hear more than one station at a time. FM broadcast radio greatly reduces this problem.

You may have noticed that while listening to an FM station in a car, the station is suddenly replaced by another. Occasionally, the receiver may flip-flop back and forth between the two stations. FM receivers do this because they are designed to lock onto the strongest signal and reject the weaker.

The flip-flop action occurs when the two signals are very close in signal strength, and the receiver is unable to "decide" which signal is stronger. The FM receiver's ability to do this is known as the capture effect. This capture effect is a distinct FM advantage. It is a disadvantage if the desired signal is the weaker of the two signals.eive!
Most AM receivers will operate adequately (not necessarily well) without the need of any RF amplifier. FM receivers, on the other hand, require an RF amplification stage.

The problem is rooted in the FM receiver's inherent ability to function with signals as small as 1 microvolt. Specifically, noise reduction capabilities in FM receivers allow the receiver to tune to and process tiny RF signals, where AM receivers, for example, normally require an RF signal of about 30 microvolts.

Because noise levels increase as signal strength decreases, the smaller the signal the more noise is present. If a 1 microvolt signal is injected into the mixer of an FM receiver, the high noise level would destroy the intelligence. Consequently, it is necessary to increase the gain of the signal to at least

From the perspective of transmission, this is all very beneficial. FM transmitters are able to broadcast at much lower signal levels than AM or SSB transmitters. Add to this that FM is amplitude constant, which also decreases the need for high power transmitters. This significantly reduces operating costs.

As with your studies of AM receivers, FM receivers have components either partially or fully unique to itself. Comparing a block diagram of an FM receiver with a SSB or AM receiver will certainly reveal many likenesses; indeed, much is identical.

Still, there are sections that exist in one receiver that do not exist in others. Additionally, beyond the scope of hardware, there are conceptual differences that have given rise to terminology not used in other systems. A firm understanding of the terms and the circuits or concepts they describe will facilitate your comprehension of FM radio.
As previously discussed, the noise rejection capability of FM is one of its essential attributes. Unfortunately, as the frequency of the intelligence rises, this aspect of FM begins to deteriorate.

Consider a live concert. High notes produced by a flute may seem to have the same energy level as a bass guitar; when, in reality, it may contain less than half the electrical energy. In FM, half the electrical energy equates to half the deviation.

This translates to much higher noise levels for all frequencies in the upper limits of the human ear. To compensate for this, nearly all FM broadcasts increase the signal strength of the upper frequencies. This particular form of signal manipulation is known as preemphasis.

Preemphasis is accomplished prior to the signal being modulated. Ultimately, the goal of preemphasis is to raise the S/N ratio of the upper frequencies to a level where noise is no longer a hindrance to high fidelity.

This is all done with respect to the desired level of the lower frequencies. The down side to preemphasis is that it disrupts the natural balance between the high and low frequencies at the receiving end.
In order to preserve this balance the signal must first be restored to its original condition. This is accomplished by the use of a deemphasis circuit in the receiver.

Deemphasis reduces the signal strength of the upper frequencies by the same amount that they were increased prior to transmission. Normally, deemphasis circuitry is located between the discriminator and the audio amplifiers.

As you may recall, the circuitry in an AM receiver that extracts the intelligence from the 455 kHz IF signal is called a Detector. In FM radios, the equivalent circuitry is usually known as a Discriminator.
It provides an intelligence signal whose amplitude is a response to the instantaneous deviations of the carrier frequency.
There are several versions of the Discriminator circuit found in FM receivers. The choice of discriminator is predominantly based on cost and technology.

For example, the Slope Detector is simplistic and inexpensive, where the Quadrature Detector and Phase Lock Loop FM Detector is best suited for implementation in IC's. Some other popular detectors are the Foster-Seely Detector and the Ratio Detector.

As in AM, Discriminators are located after the tank circuit in the final IF stage. In FM, a limiter will proceed it as well. The tank circuit is detuned from the carrier in order that the carrier is in the most linear portion of the response curve.

As the FM signal rises above or falls below the carrier frequency, the output amplitude rises and falls in a corresponding manner. The result is an AM signal which is then detected by the diode prior to the audio amplifier(s).
Limiters perform the job of maintaining a constant amplitude for any input above value. In the FM receiver, it clips off any undesired amplitude modulation and/or amplitude spikes manifest by noise.

Limiters also provide an additional function in that they produce an AGC effect. This is accomplished because signals from the established minimum and maximum values provide a constant input level to the discriminator.
Prescaling is dividing the frequency down to a more usable, or workable value. The Nida FM receiver does not need a prescaler circuit. The PLL is capable of handling FM broadcast RF.

DISCUSSION
Aside from the components necessary to support and interface correctly with the receiver's nominal frequency range and optional circuits, AM and FM receivers are fundamentally the same.

Refer to the diagram below. Since the discriminator is essentially a demodulator, it's function is the same as an AM detector. That only leaves the Limiter and Deemphasis Network as items uniquely FM.

We have already discussed the importance of an RF amplifier stage in an FM receiver. There are two other significant advantages to having an RF stage: 1. Higher degree of Image Frequency rejection 2. Reduction of Local Oscillator Reradiation

While the superheterodyne receiver solves many of the problems that faced the TRF receivers of old, the mixer-oscillator circuitry sometimes allows unwanted signals to enter the IF amplifier.

Suppose a receiver is tuned to 27 MHz with a 1 MHz IF. The Local Oscillator or VCO would then adjust to 28 MHz. If there is an undesired station broadcasting at 29 MHz, it is quite possible that frequency may enter the mixer.
Although the receiver is tuned to the center frequency of 27 MHz, the response curve of the tuning circuit may not completely attenuate the frequency at 29 MHz.

The real problem arises when the 29 MHz frequency is fed into the mixer. The 29 MHz frequency mixes with the local oscillator's 28 MHz. That produces a difference frequency of 1 MHz --- the same as the IF!

This all results with two frequencies (27 MHz and 29 MHz) being accepted by the IF, which see either frequency as being acceptable. At this point, the undesired station may interfere with the other or completely block it.
A well designed RF amplifier with its own tunable circuit will segregate and strengthen the tuned frequency to a degree that it will fully override any image frequency that may slip into the mixer.

Reradiation of the local oscillator is normally much less of a problem, but it does occur. Basically, the LO signal is coupled back to the antenna which produces interference. Again, the inclusion of an RF amplifier stage reduces the chances of this dramatically.
Local Oscillator, Mixer and IF Amplifier:

The local oscillator, mixer and IF amplifier in an FM receiver works exactly the same as in an AM receiver. The only real difference is that the IF is standard at 10.7 MHz as opposed to 455 kHz in AM receivers.

Also, FM receivers normally incorporate two or more IF amplifier stages which increases gain and provides better filtering action so that only the desired signal is passed into the discriminator. Beyond mentioning that higher frequencies are involved, there is little reason to elaborate.

As was discussed earlier, the limiter's primary function is to provide a constant output above a certain value. Based on the limiter's circuitry, a certain voltage input must be achieved before the circuit is able to begin its limiting action.

This voltage level is called the threshold, quieting or limiting knee voltage. Once this voltage level is achieved (commonly, this voltage is about 1 volt) the limiter then begins providing a constant amplitude output, the level of which is determined by the maximum and minimum value prescribed by the limiter's range.

It should be remembered that although the FM discriminator and the AM detector strive to perform the same function, for example, the extraction of audio intelligence from the IF signal, they are not the same circuits nor, for the most part, are they interchangeable.

Although, in a pinch, an AM receiver could be used to receive an FM signal by detuning the tank circuit that precedes the detector. The name discriminator was coined because of the FM "detector's" inherent ability to discriminate between signal and noise.

The noise level in the output voltage of an FM detector results from unwanted phase modulation mentioned earlier in this lesson. The noise increases proportionally with the frequency, roughly 6 dB per octave.
OCTAVE - A range of frequency where the highest frequency is twice the lowest frequency.
DEFINITION

The insertion of a deemphasis stage immediately following the discriminator that attenuates at 6 dB per octave, curtails the noise proportionally with the frequency and restores the original S/N ratio. The frequency characteristics of the deemphasis network should be a mirror image of the preemphasis network in the transmitter.

As in AM receivers, FM receivers require having the detected intelligence amplified. There are no special requirements for the AF power amps in an FM receiver. They are much the same as any found in a home stereo system.

It may be useful to remember that stereo receivers require two amplifiers in the AF stage, one for each channel. In this instance, they should be as characteristically identical to one another as possible. Any differences in impedance or other values may cause stress to one or both of the amplifiers.

The FM frequency band of 88 to 108 MHz allows for 100 channels spaced 200 kHz apart with a frequency range from 50 to 15 kHz. The frequency deviation ratio is 5. This indicates that there will be five significant sidebands above and below the carrier frequency.
150 kHz. The additional 50 kHz provides 25 kHz guard bands at the upper and lower boundaries of each channel's frequency. These bands guard against adjacent channel interference.

Frequency modulation will result whenever the inductance or capacitance of an LC tank circuit is varied. When the variation is directly proportional to the voltage of the modulation circuit, pure FM is produced.
The circuit below illustrates a capacitor microphone FM Generator. The microphone is a commonplace item found on many portable cassette recorders and is often referred to as a condenser microphone.
Ultimately, it is nothing more than a variable capacitor. In the absence of sound waves, the capacitor's plates are static and there is no change in capacitive value.

However, when sound waves strike the orifice of the microphone the plates move in and out accordingly, causing the capacitance to increase or decrease from whatever fixed capacitive value is in place.

When the changing capacitive value directly affects the oscillator's frequency, two factors may be realized: 1. The intelligence amplitude determines the rate of frequency deviation. 2. The intelligence frequency determines the amount of frequency deviation.

Manual Tuning circuitry will vary to some degree from one receiver to another. This is primarily due to the whim of whatever engineer designed the receiver, and also due to component availability.
Potentiometer R1 performs manual tuning when selected.riable resistor R1 is the actual tuning control used for frequency selection. As the knob is rotated clockwise, the voltage increases.
This voltage crosses S1, the Tuning Select Switch (which will be in the DOWN position for manual operation) and feeds up to the filter consisting of D2, L1.

D2 is a Varactor which is a specialized diode primarily used for its voltage controlled variable capacitance. Varactors have replaced the mechanically tuned capacitors which where the mainstay of older receivers.

As the voltage level increases across D2, its capacitance decreases, which, in turn, increases the frequency. Remember, all local radio frequencies are interfacing with the antenna at any given moment of time. It's the job of the filter to pass only the desired frequency.
Note the tank circuit formed by varactor D1 and variable inductor L2. This circuit provides a reference frequency for the voltage controlled oscillator. It, too, is controlled by the voltage from R1.

This means that both circuits simultaneously tune to the same frequency. It is critical for these two circuits to work together, any frequency difference will cause tracking errors. The local oscillator must be precisely at 10.7 MHz below the tuned RF, otherwise stations will appear on the dial where they shouldn't be.
While exact tuning between the RF and the local oscillator is desired, achieving it is not possible; there will always be some measurable error.
A receiver's ability to faithfully reproduce a desired signal is based predominantly by its sensitivity and selectivity of the incoming RF signal.

The quality of those two characteristics may be affected by any number of reasons both internal and external of the receiver. Station drift, atmospheric interference, and internally generated noise are a few of the reasons for poor reception....
The use of Synthesized Tuning Loops help eliminate these problems or at least reduce them to an acceptable level.

The term "synthesis" refers to any process whereby separate elements are combined to create or form a coherent whole. This is exactly what frequency synthesis does. It generates a large number of stable frequencies (in some pre-established range) while actually using only a few oscillators and, in most cases, only one...
Simply stated, a Phase-Lock Loop system compares the output of a Voltage Controlled Oscillator (VCO) with an established reference frequency.
If the output is in error, a DC controlling voltage is produced to steer the VCO output.

The VCO was first addressed in the discussion of the RF section of the receiver. Unlike normal crystal oscillators which operate at a set frequency, the frequency of the oscillator in a VCO is variable based on the voltage applied to its tuning capacitor (the previously mentioned varactor) at the input of the VCO.
Phase Detectors may be categorized into two broad groups; sequential circuits and multiplier circuits.

Multipliers provide a DC error output as the product of the reference frequency times the input frequency. A well designed multiplier is capable of phase lock on signals residing in electronically noisy environments.

Sequential phase detectors are normally designed using digital circuits and, in effect, have memory. This is not true with multipliers, which are zero-memory devices. The output voltage generated by sequential phase detectors is the result of the time interval between the zero crossing of the two frequencies.
With the memory capability of sequential detectors, they are capable of providing phase detection characteristics that are not normally obtainable when multiplier circuits are used.
The Phase Detector used on the PC130-438, PC130-441 and PC130-444 circuit cards is a tri-state, sequential device, Its job is to compare reference frequency against the incoming frequency of the VCO.

When the frequency and phase of the two signals are equal, PD out, located at pin 5, is in a high impedance state. When the VCO's output (fv) is greater than reference frequency (fr) the phase detector outputs negative pulses. When fv is smaller than fr, the phase detector outputs positive pulses.

Most counters, however, are best suited for operation in the 100 MHz range or lower. This problem has already been addressed.
The last major component of the phase-lock loop is the loop filter. It is usually a simple low-pass filter but is very important to the overall operation of the PLL.
The filter's primary goal is to remove any harmonic components of the reference frequency as well as any noise elements that may be, and normally are, present.
